script: A group at a Norwegian institute set out to test whether the order of questions on a survey changes the answers people give. They recruited 2,100 respondents and gave half of them a questionnaire about local services with the housing questions first, and the other half the same questionnaire with the transport questions first. Everything else was identical, including the wording and the response scales. Satisfaction with transport was rated more than half a point higher, on a seven-point scale, when transport came first. Satisfaction with housing barely moved. The researchers suggest that respondents answer early questions with more care and later ones by reference to what they have already said, so the first topic gets an independent judgement and the rest get a comparison. They note that this explanation predicts a further result they did not design for and did observe: the effect was larger among respondents who completed the survey quickly. The team is explicit that their finding does not show that survey results are worthless. It shows that a difference of half a point between two surveys may be a difference in question order, and that neither survey can tell you which.

items.stem: What did the two versions of the questionnaire differ in?
items.rationale: Everything was identical except which topic came first, including wording and response scales.

items.stem: What effect did question order have?
options: Transport was rated higher when first
Housing was rated higher when first
items.rationale: Transport satisfaction rose by more than half a point when transport came first, while housing barely moved.

items.stem: What explanation do the researchers offer?
options: Later answers are made by comparison
Respondents tire and answer at random
Housing is a less familiar subject
items.rationale: They propose that early questions get an independent judgement and later ones are answered by reference to what has already been said.

items.stem: Why is the result about fast respondents mentioned?
options: The explanation predicted it in advance
It was the study's original aim
It shows the sample was unusual
items.rationale: The passage says the explanation predicts a further result the team did not design for and did observe.

items.stem: What do the authors say their finding does NOT show?
options: That the effect can be measured
items.rationale: They are explicit that the finding does not show survey results are worthless, only that a half-point gap may be order.

script: Between 2019 and 2024 a hospital in Melbourne recorded every occasion on which a patient's discharge was delayed by more than a day, together with the reason given by the ward. The purpose was to find where the bottleneck lay, and the answer surprised the people who commissioned the work. The largest single category was not a shortage of beds elsewhere, nor transport, but the wait for a signature from a doctor who had already made the decision. In 41 per cent of delayed discharges the clinical decision had been taken on the previous ward round, and what remained was paperwork. The hospital changed one thing in response. Discharge summaries could be signed by any doctor on the treating team rather than by the consultant alone. Median delay fell from 26 hours to 9 within four months and has stayed there. The authors are careful to say that a single site cannot establish that this change caused the fall, because two other things happened in the same period, including the arrival of a new electronic record. What the data support is narrower: the bottleneck was where nobody expected it, and it was found only because the reason for each delay was recorded rather than counted.

items.stem: What was the largest cause of delayed discharge?
items.rationale: The largest single category was the wait for a signature from a doctor who had already decided.

items.stem: What proportion of delays involved a decision already taken?
items.rationale: In 41 per cent of delayed discharges the clinical decision had been taken on the previous ward round.

items.stem: What change did the hospital make?
items.rationale: Discharge summaries could be signed by any doctor on the treating team rather than by the consultant alone.

items.stem: Why can the fall not be attributed to that change?
options: Two other things changed as well
The sample was far too small
items.rationale: The authors note two other things happened in the same period, including a new electronic record.

items.stem: What made the bottleneck findable?
options: Reasons were recorded, not just counted
items.rationale: The closing sentence says it was found only because the reason for each delay was recorded rather than counted.

script: A field experiment carried out with a chain of thirty-one bakeries asked whether telling customers about waste changes what they buy. In half the shops, a sign near the till reported how many loaves had been thrown away the previous week and invited customers to buy day-old bread at a reduced price. The other shops sold the same discounted bread with no sign. Sales of day-old bread rose by 22 per cent in the shops with the sign. Total revenue did not change, because customers who bought the cheaper bread were largely those who would otherwise have bought fresh. Waste fell by about a tenth, which is less than the rise in day-old sales because the shops were already selling some of it. The interesting result is in the second half of the study. When the signs were removed after eight weeks, day-old sales stayed above their old level for a further three months, then drifted back. The authors read this as habit rather than persuasion: customers who tried the cheaper bread once continued while the reason to try it stayed in mind, and stopped when it did not.

items.stem: What did the sign report?
items.rationale: The sign near the till reported how many loaves had been thrown away the previous week.

items.stem: Why did total revenue stay the same?
items.rationale: Customers who bought the cheaper bread were largely those who would otherwise have bought fresh.

items.stem: Why did waste fall by less than sales rose?
items.rationale: Waste fell about a tenth, less than the rise in day-old sales, because the shops were already selling some of it.

items.stem: What happened after the signs were removed?
options: Sales stayed high, then drifted back
items.rationale: Day-old sales stayed above the old level for three months and then drifted back.

items.stem: How do the authors interpret that?
items.rationale: They read it as habit: customers continued while the reason stayed in mind and stopped when it did not.

script: The proposition that bilingual children develop stronger executive control than monolingual children entered textbooks with unusual speed, and it has spent the last decade being taken apart in a manner that is instructive quite apart from the question itself. The original studies were small, and they were conducted in settings where bilingual and monolingual groups differed in more than language: immigration history, household income, and the schools they attended. Later work with larger samples and closer matching found the advantage shrinking as the matching improved, which is the signature of a confound rather than of an effect. A registered analysis pooling nineteen datasets found no reliable difference on the standard measures. That would be the end of it, except that the same analysis found something the original literature had not looked for. Among children who switched languages frequently within a conversation, rather than simply speaking two, a small association with one measure of switching cost survived matching. The authors are appropriately cautious: it is one measure among several, the association is weak, and the group was not defined in advance. What the episode demonstrates is that a finding can be false as stated and still be pointing at something, and that the way to tell is not to defend the original claim but to specify a narrower one and test it as if it were new. The reception of the retraction is itself part of the record: the shrunken claim travelled to a small fraction of the places the original had reached, and a survey of introductory textbooks four years after the pooled analysis found that eleven of the nineteen still stated the advantage as established. That gap between what a field believes and what it has shown is not a failure of any individual, and it is not corrected by publishing more carefully. It is corrected, slowly, by whoever writes the next textbook reading the analysis rather than the abstract of the study it replaced.

items.stem: What was wrong with the original studies?
options: The samples were far too old
items.rationale: Bilingual and monolingual groups differed in immigration history, income and schooling as well as language.

items.stem: What does the shrinking advantage indicate?
options: A confound rather than an effect
items.rationale: The passage calls the advantage shrinking as matching improved the signature of a confound.

items.stem: What did the pooled analysis find on standard measures?
items.rationale: The registered analysis pooling nineteen datasets found no reliable difference on the standard measures.

items.stem: What survived the matching?
options: An effect in older children only
items.rationale: Among children who switched languages frequently within a conversation, a weak association with one switching-cost measure survived.

items.stem: What lesson does the writer draw?
options: Specify a narrower claim and test it afresh
Defend the original claim more carefully
items.rationale: The closing sentence says the way to tell is to specify a narrower claim and test it as if it were new.

script: When a government agency in Chile began publishing the individual inspection scores of food premises rather than a pass or fail, researchers were handed a natural experiment that is difficult to arrange deliberately. The scores had always existed; only their visibility changed, and it changed on a date the agency chose for administrative reasons unrelated to the premises themselves. In the eighteen months that followed, average scores rose by roughly nine per cent, and the rise came almost entirely from premises that had previously been scoring just above the pass threshold. Those already scoring well did not improve, and those far below did not either. The pattern is what a model of reputational pressure predicts, and it is not what a model of enforcement predicts, since enforcement did not change. A second finding complicates the picture. The number of premises inspected fell by fourteen per cent over the same period, because inspections took longer once inspectors knew their numbers would be published and began documenting each judgement more carefully. The agency therefore bought an improvement among the marginal at the price of visiting fewer premises overall, and the study cannot say whether the trade was worth making, because it has no measure of illness. What it can say is that publishing a number changed the behaviour of the people being measured and the people doing the measuring, and that only the first of those was intended. A final observation belongs with the others because it was not part of the design. Premises that closed during the period were, on average, scoring slightly below those that stayed open, but the difference is small and the closures are too few to support any claim about cause. The agency has since asked whether publication should be extended to the inspection interval itself, which would make visible the fourteen per cent the study found, and that is the rare case of a measurement problem being answered by publishing the measurement that revealed it.

items.stem: What changed on the chosen date?
items.rationale: The scores had always existed and only their visibility changed, on a date chosen for unrelated administrative reasons.

items.stem: Which premises improved?
options: Those just above the pass mark
items.rationale: The rise came almost entirely from premises previously scoring just above the pass threshold.

items.stem: Why does the pattern favour reputational pressure?
items.rationale: The writer notes the pattern fits reputational pressure and not enforcement, since enforcement did not change.

items.stem: Why did the number of inspections fall?
options: Each one took longer to document
items.rationale: Inspections took longer once inspectors knew their numbers would be published and documented each judgement more carefully.

items.stem: Why can the study not judge the trade-off?
items.rationale: The passage states the study cannot say whether the trade was worth making because it has no measure of illness.

script: For thirty years the received account of how the Polynesian islands were settled rested on radiocarbon dates from charcoal and shell, and it described a slow eastward drift over a millennium. The account has been revised twice, and the second revision is more interesting than the first. The first came from re-examining what was being dated. Charcoal from long-lived wood can be centuries older than the fire that burned it, and shell takes carbon from seawater whose age varies by region. When dating was restricted to short-lived plant material, the settlement of East Polynesia contracted from about a thousand years to roughly two hundred and fifty. The second revision came from a different direction entirely. Sediment cores taken from island lakes record the arrival of introduced species, and those records are continuous rather than dependent on what happened to be excavated. In three cases the cores show human presence a generation or two before the earliest reliable radiocarbon date from any site on the same island. The gap is small and consistent, and the explanation offered is unglamorous: the first arrivals leave little that survives, and archaeology finds settlements rather than landings. The revised chronology is therefore not simply shorter than the old one. It is shorter at one end and slightly earlier at the other, and the two corrections came from methods that share no assumptions. One consequence deserves stating plainly, because it is easy to miss in a chronology argument. A settlement period of two hundred and fifty years rather than a thousand describes a different kind of undertaking: not a drift, but a deliberate and sustained programme of voyaging carried out within about ten generations. The archaeology did not change to produce that conclusion. What changed was the discipline's willingness to distrust its own most abundant material, which had been abundant precisely because it survives, and to prefer the scarcer material that dates what it is supposed to date.

items.stem: What was the problem with the original dating?
options: Too few sites had been excavated
items.rationale: Charcoal from long-lived wood can be centuries older than the fire, and shell carbon varies by region.

items.stem: What happened when short-lived material was used?
options: The dates moved several centuries later
items.rationale: East Polynesian settlement contracted from about a thousand years to roughly two hundred and fifty.

items.stem: What advantage do the sediment cores have?
items.rationale: The cores are continuous rather than dependent on what happened to be excavated.

items.stem: What do the cores show in three cases?
options: Arrival slightly before the earliest site date
items.rationale: They show human presence a generation or two before the earliest reliable radiocarbon date from any site on the island.

items.stem: Why does the writer stress the two methods?
options: They were used by one team
They rely on the same cores
items.rationale: The final sentence notes the two corrections came from methods that share no assumptions.

script: An unusually direct test of whether open-plan offices increase collaboration became possible when two large firms moved their headquarters and agreed to let researchers fit staff with sensors that recorded face-to-face interaction and, separately, to log volumes of internal email and messaging. The expectation, stated in both firms' own planning documents, was that removing walls would raise face-to-face contact. It fell. In one firm, time in face-to-face interaction dropped by roughly seventy per cent after the move; in the other, by about half. Electronic messaging rose by a comparable amount in both. The authors resist the reading that open plan simply fails, and their reason is worth following. A person in an open space has lost the ability to control who overhears them and gained the ability to see whether a colleague looks busy. Both changes push the same way: conversation that would once have been a two-minute exchange at a desk becomes a message, because the message is private and does not require a judgement about whether now is a good moment. The finding is therefore not that people collaborated less, which the study cannot measure, but that they moved the collaboration somewhere the walls no longer governed. Whether the substitution costs anything depends on what the exchanges were for, and neither firm had any record of that before the move. There is a further asymmetry the sensors captured and the planning documents had not anticipated. The fall in face-to-face contact was not evenly distributed across the two firms' staff: it was largest among those whose work required concentration in long blocks, and smallest among those whose work was already interruption-driven. If the purpose of removing walls was to make the second group talk more, it barely moved them, and it moved the first group a great deal in the opposite direction. That is the shape of an intervention aimed at an average that describes very few of the people in it.

items.stem: What did both firms expect from the move?
items.rationale: Both firms' planning documents stated the expectation that removing walls would raise face-to-face contact.

items.stem: What actually happened to face-to-face interaction?
options: It fell substantially in both firms
It rose in one firm only
items.rationale: It dropped by roughly seventy per cent in one firm and about half in the other.

items.stem: What two changes does the writer identify?
options: Losing privacy and gaining sight of others
Losing desks and gaining meeting rooms
items.rationale: A person loses control over who overhears and gains the ability to see whether a colleague looks busy.

items.stem: Why do those changes favour messaging?
options: A message is private and untimed
items.rationale: The passage says a message is private and does not require judging whether now is a good moment.

items.stem: What can the study not determine?
items.rationale: Whether the substitution costs anything depends on what the exchanges were for, and neither firm had a record of that.
